title: The Five Key Beliefs Beneath Student Motivation
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: This guide serves as Dave Stuart Jr.'s master overview of the Five Key Beliefs framework, Credibility, Value, Effort, Efficacy, and Belonging, which he presents as the psychological roots common to motivated classrooms regardless of subject, pedagogy, or demographics. He explains five critical qualities of the beliefs: they are knowledge held in the will rather than the intellect, they exist on a spectrum rather than as binary states, they are hierarchically interrelated, they are context-dependent, and they are malleable even through brief interventions. From there he traces how his original 55-strategy draft for The Will to Learn was pared down to 10 core strategies, each mapped to the belief or beliefs it cultivates. The piece functions as a hub, linking out to Stuart's deeper one-stop-shop guides on each individual belief and strategy.
points: Stuart's central claim is that the path to the head, it turns out, is through the heart, meaning cognitive learning is gated by these five underlying motivational beliefs.

The beliefs are hierarchically interrelated: he recommends building from Credibility first, since it is especially malleable and the point of best leverage, rather than starting with Belonging as many teachers do.

Because beliefs are context-dependent, the same student can be highly motivated in one class and disengaged in another, which Stuart frames as good news since teachers control a sliver of context that is massively influential.
The article documents Stuart's editorial discipline: cutting an original 55-strategy list down to a memorable 10, each tied explicitly to specific beliefs.
quotes: Credibility, Value, Effort, Efficacy, and Belonging — these are the roots of student motivation, which presents itself as care-driven, learning-conducive behaviors.
The Five Key Beliefs pave the path to the head. Because the path to the head, it turns out, is through the heart.

What I always tell teachers who are getting started is focus on Credibility. It's especially malleable, it's the most within your control, and it's the point of best leverage from which to influence the other beliefs.
How we shape the school or classroom context is enormously predictive of the degree to which students will pursue mastery with care. And we shape that context every day, during every encounter.
This means that comments like so-and-so is just an unmotivated student aren't accurate or helpful because they disempower the teacher to do the kinds of things that influence student motivation.
In the subsequent draft, I took the initial list of 55 strategies and reduced it to just 10.
